extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, mathematics educators, students and readers interested in mathematical style, pedagogy, and philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Epigrammatic guidelines and normative statements about how mathematics should be taught, written, and valued — emphasizing clarity, connection to physics/applications, and understanding underlying ideas rather than formalistic axiomatics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value determined by significance and usefulness, not difficulty
rubrics_metrics.description: “The value of a mathematical achievement is determined, not by its significance and usefulness as in other sciences, but by its difficulty alone, as in mountaineering.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold criticizes the view (attributed to a 'democratic principle' advanced in mathematics) that prizes difficulty over significance; he argues this leads to misguided priorities and separation from other sciences (quote from 'Will Mathematics Survive? Report on the Zurich Congress', The Mathematical Intelligencer, 1995).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain connection between mathematics and physics/natural sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: “In the middle of the twentieth century it was attempted to divide physics and mathematics. The consequences turned out to be catastrophic.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold warns that divorcing mathematics from physics and the natural sciences produces generations of mathematicians ignorant of large parts of their science; pedagogy and research should preserve links to scientific applications (see 'On teaching mathematics', Russian Mathematical Surveys, 1998).

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach with motivation; avoid 'ugly scholastic pseudo-mathematics'
rubrics_metrics.description: “They first began teaching their ugly scholastic pseudo-mathematics to their students, then to schoolchildren (forgetting Hardy's warning that ugly mathematics has no permanent place under the Sun).”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid presenting unmotivated axioms and definitions that make the subject hard to master for the uninitiated; prioritize motivating concepts and intelligibility in textbooks and instruction (Arnold, 'On teaching mathematics').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use clear, natural language instead of needless formalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast between prose like “Petya washed his hands” and convoluted formalized sentences: Arnold finds it almost impossible to read contemporary mathematicians who replace simple statements with long formal mappings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer simple, direct wording in mathematical exposition. The page quotes a formalized paragraph as an anti-pattern, urging authors to avoid replacing natural statements with overformalized technical sentences (Conversation with Arnold, The Mathematical Intelligencer, 1987).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure students master proofs early to recognize correct reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: “A person, who had not mastered the art of the proofs in high school, is as a rule unable to distinguish correct reasoning from that which is misleading.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes teaching proof techniques early in education so learners can discriminate correct from misleading arguments; failure to do so makes people vulnerable to manipulation (from 'The antiscientifical revolution and mathematics', 1998).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive axiomization and abstraction that causes illegibility
rubrics_metrics.description: “The axiomization and algebraization of mathematics, after more than 50 years, has led to the illegibility so such a large number of mathematical texts that the threat of complete loss of contact with physics and the natural sciences has been realized.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns against heavy formal axiomatics and algebraization which render texts unintelligible to many readers and sever ties to applications; favor clarity, examples, and motivation over abstract generality (V. I. Arnold, Geometrical Methods...).

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on underlying problems, conjectures, and ideas behind theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogy: when collecting mushrooms you see only the fruit, but a mycologist knows the large structure beneath; in mathematics, theorems are the 'fruit' while problems, conjectures, mistakes, and ideas are what lie beneath.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages mathematicians and students to look beyond isolated theorems to the deeper questions and conceptual structures that connect results; teaching and exposition should reveal these connections (Mathematical Events of the Twentieth Century excerpt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Value empirical/physical intuition; mathematics as physics with cheap experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: “Mathematics is the part of physics where experiments are cheap.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supports using experimentation, physical intuition, and application-driven thinking in mathematical work and pedagogy; aligns with Arnold's broader call to keep mathematics connected to the sciences ('On teaching mathematics', Russian Mathematical Surveys, 1998).

rubrics_metrics.name: Present principles in an understandable manner in textbooks
rubrics_metrics.description: “In almost all textbooks, even the best, this principle is presented so that it is impossible to understand.” (referring to a principle in classical material)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textbook authors should avoid presenting central principles in obfuscated ways; clarity of presentation is essential for comprehension (quote referencing K. Jacobi, with Arnold's remark in Mathematical Methods of Classical Mechanics).
